paras.text: Sitework, Concrete, and Foundations — Audio Lecture

This chapter covers the biggest single block of your trade exam: excavation and sitework, site engineering, concrete, and footings and foundations. Together that is thirty-two of the one hundred ten trade questions — almost one in three. Everything here comes from the twenty-fifteen Michigan Residential Code, chapter four, plus the MISS DIG law and MIOSHA excavation rules. The exam is closed book, so these numbers have to live in your head. Let's build them in the order a real job happens: engineer the site, dig, form and pour, then protect the foundation.

Start with the site. Before anyone digs, you read the plot plan. It shows property lines, setbacks, easements, the building footprint, utilities, well and septic, and contour lines. Two definitions the exam loves. A benchmark is a permanent point of known elevation — vertical control, your starting point for all height measurements. A monument is a permanent marker of a property corner or boundary — horizontal control — and disturbing one is illegal. Don't mix them up. Contour lines connect points of equal elevation. Close together means steep, far apart means flat, and contour lines never cross.

Here is the leveling math, because they will make you do it. Set the instrument, shoot the benchmark. Height of instrument equals the benchmark elevation plus that backsight reading. Then any point's elevation equals height of instrument minus the foresight reading at that point. Say the benchmark is one hundred point zero, the backsight is four and a half feet, so the height of instrument is one hundred four and a half. Foresight at the garage corner reads six and a quarter. One hundred four and a half minus six and a quarter is ninety-eight and a quarter. And remember the logic check: a higher rod reading means lower ground.

Rural site engineering means well and septic. A percolation test measures how fast water drains through soil, in minutes per inch, to size a septic drain field. Too slow — think dense clay, slower than about sixty minutes per inch — and it fails. The numbers: a one-thousand-gallon tank minimum regardless of flow — that one is in the state E G L E criteria — with twelve fifty for four bedrooms as common local practice. The state well code minimum is fifty feet from a single-family well to both the septic tank and the drain field, though many local health departments push the drain field to seventy-five or one hundred feet. Tank ten feet from the foundation and drain field twenty feet are local practice numbers. Well casing runs at least twenty-five feet below grade and sticks up twelve inches above grade — that one is state well code, rule R three twenty-five point sixteen thirty-two.

Now, before a single bucket of dirt moves in Michigan, you call MISS DIG. Dial eight one one at least three full working days before excavating. Working days — not calendar days, not seventy-two hours. That's Public Act one seventy-four of twenty thirteen. Fail to call and you face a civil fine of up to five thousand dollars. Knowingly damaging or hiding utility marks — that's the misdemeanor, not the failure to call. And MISS DIG only marks member utility lines. The homeowner's private lines — the run to the detached garage, the well feed — those are on you. Know the colors: red is electric, yellow is gas or oil, orange is telecom, blue is water, green is sewer, white is your own proposed dig, pink is survey, purple is reclaimed water.

Trench safety. Four depth numbers, and the exam will try to make you swap them. At four feet deep you need a ladder or ramp within twenty-five feet of lateral travel. At five feet deep you need a protective system — sloping, benching, shoring, or a trench box — unless you are in stable rock. At twenty feet deep, the protective system must be designed by a registered professional engineer. And keep your spoil pile and equipment at least two feet back from the edge. One more contrast: six feet is the fall-protection trigger. Five feet is the trench trigger. Different rules, different numbers.

Soil types. Stable rock can stand vertical. Type A is stiff clay, one and a half tons per square foot or more — slope it three-quarters to one, fifty-three degrees. Type B is medium soils — slope one to one, forty-five degrees. Type C is sand, gravel, or anything submerged or seeping — slope one and a half to one, thirty-four degrees. The weaker the soil, the flatter the slope. And here's the trap: you can never bench Type C soil. Benching is for A and B only. Every excavation needs a competent person — someone who can identify hazards and has authority to fix them — inspecting daily and after every rain.

Michigan sitework has one more permit trap. A soil erosion and sedimentation control permit — Part ninety-one of the natural resources act — is triggered by disturbing one acre or more, or any earth change within five hundred feet of a lake or stream. Wetlands are a different program entirely, Part three-oh-three. If the question says wetland, the answer is not Part ninety-one.

On to bearing soil. Footings sit on undisturbed natural soil or engineered fill — never on organic muck, loose fill, or frozen ground. Presumptive bearing values, from best to worst: crystalline bedrock, twelve thousand pounds per square foot. Sedimentary rock, four thousand. Sandy gravel, three thousand. Sand, two thousand. Clay and silt, fifteen hundred. Compaction gets verified against a Proctor test — the lab finds the soil's maximum dry density, and the field spec is usually ninety to ninety-five percent of it.

Now the foundation itself, and the single most Michigan number on this exam: forty-two inches. All exterior footings and foundation systems extend forty-two inches below actual grade. That's a Michigan amendment — the generic I R C answer of twelve inches below grade is a trap. The exemptions: freestanding accessory buildings up to six hundred square feet of light-frame construction, or four hundred square feet of heavier construction, with eaves ten feet or less — and freestanding decks not attached to the house.

Footing dimensions. Minimum thickness, six inches. The footing projects at least two inches beyond each face of the wall, and that projection can never exceed the footing's own thickness. Width comes from the code tables based on soil strength and stories — twelve inches is the everyday light-frame answer on decent soil, and it widens as soil weakens. The top of a footing must be level. The bottom can slope up to one in ten — ten percent — and steeper than that, you step the footing. Building next to a slope steeper than one vertical in three horizontal — thirty-three percent — triggers special setback rules.

Anchor bolts — drill this string until it's automatic. Half-inch diameter minimum. Six feet on center maximum. Seven inches embedded into the concrete or grouted block. At least two bolts per plate section, one within twelve inches of each end, sitting in the middle third of the plate width, nut and washer tightened. And a trap to disarm: the four-foot spacing for buildings over two stories is a seismic rule for design categories C and D — Michigan is category A or B, so six feet on center governs no matter how many stories. Same reason you do not need those big three-by-three plate washers — that's an earthquake-country rule.

Foundation walls: thickness comes from tables driven by wall height, unbalanced backfill height, and soil class. The wall must stick up above finished grade at least four inches where masonry veneer is used, six inches everywhere else. And never backfill until the wall has cured and is braced or anchored to the floor framing above — then backfill in six to twelve inch compacted lifts of clean material.

Keeping the basement dry is three separate systems, and the exam tests whether you can tell them apart. First, surface grading: the ground falls six inches in the first ten feet away from the foundation — impervious surfaces need two percent. Second, foundation drains: drain tile or perforated pipe at or below the top of the footing, discharging by gravity or pump to an approved outlet. The gravel over the drain extends one full foot beyond the outside edge of the footing and six inches above the top of the footing, wrapped in filter fabric. The pipe sits on two inches of washed gravel with six inches over it. No drain needed on well-drained gravelly Group One soils. Third, the wall coating. Dampproofing is the default — from top of footing to finished grade, a bituminous coating, with masonry walls parged first with three-eighths of an inch of portland cement. Waterproofing — an actual membrane — is required only where a high water table or severe soil-water conditions are known. Dampproofing stops soil moisture. Waterproofing stops water under pressure.

Crawl spaces: vent area one square foot per one hundred fifty square feet of floor, dropping to one per fifteen hundred with a ground vapor retarder, with a vent within three feet of each corner. Access through the floor is eighteen by twenty-four inches; through a perimeter wall, sixteen by twenty-four. Floor is bigger — eighteen. Wall is sixteen.

Concrete. All of Michigan is severe weathering, so learn three strengths. Twenty-five hundred p s i for footings, interior slabs, and foundation walls not exposed to weather. Three thousand for vertical concrete exposed to weather. Thirty-five hundred for garage floor slabs, porches, carport slabs, and steps — anything that sees deicing salt. And every piece of exterior concrete gets air entrainment, five to seven percent — those microscopic bubbles give freezing water room to expand.

Mix basics: water-cement ratio around point four five to point five zero. Adding water on site raises the slump but kills strength. A slump test measures workability — four to six inches is normal residential, footings often two to four. Admixtures: accelerators for cold weather — but never calcium chloride around embedded or prestressed steel, because chlorides corrode it. Retarders for hot weather and long hauls. Water reducers for workability without extra water. Air entrainers for freeze-thaw.

Steel placement is a classic discrimination question. Footing rebar goes in the bottom third — the tension zone — with three inches of cover where cast against earth. Welded wire mesh in a slab goes in the upper third, on chairs — mesh lying in the dirt does nothing. Bar sizes are eighths of an inch: number three is three-eighths, number four is a half inch, number five is five-eighths.

Finishing sequence: screed, bull float, then stop and let the bleed water evaporate. Never finish bleed water back into the surface. Then edge, cut your joints, float, trowel — interior only, because a steel trowel makes exterior concrete dangerously slick — and broom finish outside for traction. Control joints get cut at least a quarter of the slab depth, spaced roughly eight to twelve feet on a four-inch slab. Isolation joints separate the slab from walls and columns. Construction joints end a day's pour.

Curing and cold weather: concrete hits about seventy percent of design strength at seven days and full design strength at twenty-eight. Keep it moist and around fifty degrees. In cold weather, never pour on frozen ground, and protect fresh concrete from freezing until it reaches five hundred p s i — roughly the first forty-eight to seventy-two hours. Interior slabs: three and a half inches thick minimum, over four inches of granular base, over six-mil poly. Volume math: length times width times thickness, all in feet, divided by twenty-seven gives cubic yards — and order ten percent extra.

Rapid-fire recap. Forty-two inches — Michigan frost depth. Six in ten — grade away from the house. Six inches — footing thickness; two inches — footing projection. Half inch, six feet, seven inches, two per plate, twelve from the end — anchor bolts. Four with veneer, six otherwise — wall above grade. One foot beyond, six above — drain gravel. Twenty-five hundred, three thousand, thirty-five hundred — footings, exposed walls, garage slabs. Five to seven percent air. Four to six slump. Seven days, seventy percent; twenty-eight days, full strength. Fifty degrees and five hundred p s i for cold weather. Three and a half inch slab, four inch base, six mil poly. One-fifty crawl venting; eighteen by twenty-four floor, sixteen by twenty-four wall. Fifteen hundred, two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, twelve thousand — clay, sand, gravel, sedimentary rock, bedrock. Eight one one, three working days, five thousand dollar fine. Four feet ladder, five feet protection, two feet spoil, twenty feet engineer. Fifty-three, forty-five, thirty-four degrees — A, B, C — and you never bench Type C. One acre or five hundred feet of water — erosion permit. Fifty feet, tank to well; one thousand gallons for three bedrooms. Nail these and you own the biggest block on the exam.
